With the detector configured for a nominal false-positive rate of $10^{-5}$, VOW detects 99.4% of 200-token watermarked texts with competitive text quality and practical overhead. Under explicit conditions, our oracle-assisted text construction produces detector-positive text for all three Green-Red detectors evaluated. Paraphrasing substantially weakens every scheme evaluated, limiting watermark-based FPA to relatively intact content.
item.dc:creator: Xiaokun Luan, Yihao Zhang, Pengcheng Su, Feiran Lei, Kailong Wang, Guangdong Bai, Meng Sun

item.title: Few-Shot Truly Benign DPO Attack for Jailbreaking LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2605.10998v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fine-tuning APIs make frontier LLMs easy to customize, but they can also weaken safety alignment during fine-tuning. While prior work shows that benign supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can reduce refusal behavior, deployed fine-tuning pipelines increasingly support preference-based objectives, whose safety risks remain less understood. We show that Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) introduces a stronger and harder-to-audit failure mode. We propose a truly benign DPO attack using only 10 harmless preference pairs, the minimum data scale accepted by OpenAI's fine-tuning service. Each pair contains a benign prompt, a normal helpful answer as the preferred response, and a refusal as the dispreferred response. Unlike prior benign fine-tuning attacks, our data exhibits no suspicious behavior: it is practically indistinguishable from the fine-tuning request of a legitimate user seeking to reduce over-refusal, making harmful intent almost impossible to infer from the request alone. Nevertheless, because DPO directly optimizes the model to prefer helpful answers over refusals, this seemingly benign objective broadly suppresses refusal behavior and transfers to harmful prompts outside the fine-tuning data. Across OpenAI models supporting DPO fine-tuning, our attack achieves attack success rates of 59.13% on GPT-4o, 70.20% on GPT-4.1, 54.80% on GPT-4.1-mini, and 81.73% on GPT-4.1-nano, at costs of only \$1.7, \$1.7, \$0.3, and \$0.1. Moreover, on open-weight models that do not impose minimum data requirements, we find that this effect can emerge from even a single benign preference pair.
item.dc:creator: Sangyeon Yoon, Wonje Jeung, Yoonjun Cho, Dongjae Jeon, Albert No

item.title: SecureClaw: Clawing Back Control of LLM Agents
item.description: arXiv:2606.09549v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents face two distinct security failures: unauthorized external actions and exposure of sensitive plaintext inside the runtime before any final output check can intervene. Existing defenses usually protect one boundary, either the planner/runtime or the point where external actions are executed, and therefore do not by themselves secure both surfaces. We present SecureClaw, a dual-boundary architecture that enforces authorization in a trusted executor and keeps raw protected data outside the LLM runtime. Sensitive reads pass through a trusted gateway that replaces raw values with reference IDs. In the evaluated deployment, the gateway also provides short planning summaries that deliberately release selected information, a process called declassification. Writes that change external state follow a PREVIEW$\rightarrow$COMMIT protocol in which only a trusted executor may execute the exact request authorized by policy. The runtime can still plan over summaries and reference IDs, but cannot directly resolve the IDs into secrets or perform side effects. Across the AgentDojo, AgentLeak, and Agent Security Bench (ASB) benchmarks, SecureClaw is the only defense we evaluate in a common harness that simultaneously retains usable task utility and achieves 0% attack success rate (ASR) on ASB, 0.64% ASR on AgentDojo, and 3.23% overall leak on AgentLeak's attacked parity lane, which measures final-output and internal-relay leakage. Code is available at https://github.com/ponyyuhan/SecureClaw.
item.dc:creator: Yuhan Ma, Stefan Schmid

item.title: EvoSafeHarness: Evolving Model- and Domain-Specific Harnesses for Securing Agents
item.description: arXiv:2609.05903v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can translate natural-language requests into real-world actions, creating safety risks from both indirect prompt injections and directly harmful requests. Existing system-level safety harnesses are typically designed by experts and applied across heterogeneous models and domains, despite substantial differences in model behavior, utility tolerance, and domain-specific safety requirements. We present EvoSafeHarness, a framework for automatically synthesizing deployment-specific safety harnesses for frozen LLM agents. Given a target model and domain specification, EvoSafeHarness jointly evolves a natural-language policy and executable enforcement logic using behavioral feedback from the target model. Each candidate is additionally evaluated through fresh-context adversarial review to filter rules that depend on benchmark artifacts. Across four agent benchmark families, EvoSafeHarness achieves a stronger safety-utility frontier than fixed expert-designed defenses. On DecodingTrust-Agent, evaluated across fifteen model-domain deployments, it reduces attack success rate from 50.9% to 12.6% for direct attacks and from 40.4% to 7.4% for indirect attacks, with a 3.3-point utility cost. On AgentDojo, it achieves 82.8% utility with 0.0% attack success rate, twice the utility of CaMeL at the same zero-attack-success operating point, while the same harness transfers unchanged to unseen AgentDyn suites. It also achieves the best score on Agent-SafetyBench for every evaluated victim model and maintains an attack success rate below 18% against an adaptive PAIR-style attacker with sixteen attempts per task. Analysis of the synthesized harnesses shows that domain semantics determine which safety relations and trajectory state must be tracked, while model and runtime behavior determine how and where those relations should be enforced.
item.dc:creator: Nanxi Li, Yingzi Ma, Yulong Cao, Chong Xiang, G. Edward Suh, Bo Li, Yejin Choi, Dawn Song, Chaowei Xiao

item.title: Towards Tackling Application Logic Flaws through Autonomous Formal-Logic Modeling and Automated Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2609.10537v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Logic flaws pose significant challenges in the design and implementation of modern, semantically rich systems and applications, impacting security, privacy, and trust. These flaws are inherently tied to business-specific semantics and threat models, making their discovery and reasoning difficult and hard to scale. Real-world systems often exhibit diverse application features, complex protocol logic, and domain-specific threat models, necessitating substantial human effort and domain expertise for effective security analysis. In this paper, we introduce LL-Verifier, a novel, automated framework for identifying logic vulnerabilities built on (1) large language models for autonomous modeling, and (2) logic model checkers for rigorous reasoning. LL-Verifier processes natural language inputs, in particular protocol descriptions and security goals, to automatically generate formal logic models and properties expressed in a new logic language built on a generic logic language Maude, optimized for modeling arbitrary application-level semantics. These formal models are then converted into logical state machines, enabling exhaustive, rigorous verification through logic level model checking. This approach streamlines the analysis of diverse, application-level protocols deployed in real-world scenarios, offering automated, exhaustive, and precise reasoning within their logical constraints. We evaluated the high effectiveness, efficiency, and practicality of LL-Verifier by applying it to 27 access control protocols of widely used IoT devices, which come with vendor-specific logic flows and semantics. While LL-verifier tackles a hard problem in application security, i.e., automatic logic flaws discovery, our analysis uncovers a range of sophisticated logic vulnerabilities in IoT protocols and devices with serious security and privacy implications.
item.dc:creator: Yiwei Fang, Yichen Liu, Luyi Xing

item.title: A2ABreak: Systematic Security Analysis of the A2A Protocol
item.description: arXiv:2609.10871v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, now governed by the Linux Foundation, is an open standard that enables autonomous AI agents to discover, authenticate with, and delegate tasks to one another across organizational boundaries. Designed to complement the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for tool integration, A2A is rapidly emerging as the horizontal communication layer of the multi-agent ecosystem. Yet the protocol's security has received no systematic analysis. This paper presents A2ABreak, the first rigorous systematic security analysis of the A2A protocol. We introduce a novel framework that utilizes an LLM-assisted extraction of a verified finite-state machine directly from the natural-language specification, producing a unified model of 37 states and 76 transitions from 929 formalized statements, and then systematically reasons over this model to discover protocol-level vulnerabilities through adversarial verification, under a full-compliance assumption. Our analysis uncovers 11 new vulnerabilities, each exploitable by a specification-compliant adversary without requiring any implementation flaw. Among the findings are cross-client context injection through unprotected context identifiers, credential harvesting via multi-hop identity loss in delegation chains, and data exfiltration through rogue agents advertising unattested capability claims. A2ABreak achieves 73.3% precision and 84.6% F1 against manual expert review, while a zero-shot LLM baseline operating over the same specification produces zero confirmed findings, demonstrating that explicit formal grounding is essential for sound protocol security analysis.
item.dc:creator: Alireza Lotfi, Mirza Masfiqur Rahman, Imtiaz Karim, Elisa Bertino

item.title: An Open-Source End-to-End FHE Implementation for Privacy-Preserving Llama 3 8B Inference
item.description: arXiv:2609.12378v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cloud LLM services typically require users to send prompts to a model provider, creating a privacy risk. Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) lets a server perform inference without decrypting the input, but representing data as ciphertexts adds storage and computational overhead. In CKKS-based LLM inference, the packing scheme maps logical tensors to ciphertexts and slots. It therefore determines the ciphertext count and the homomorphic cost of linear layers, and it constrains how data pass between linear layers, attention, and nonlinear computation. As models and sequences grow, inefficient layouts accumulate encoding, compute, and layout-conversion overhead. We present Odin, an FHE inference system that co-designs ciphertext packing and model execution for Llama. Starting from a THOR-style baseline whose bottleneck is weight encoding, Odin uses a feature-major cross-layer layout to unify residual connections and layer interfaces, and builds transient intra-operator layouts for linear projections and attention. This reduces redundant plaintext encoding of weights in wide projections. Within attention, QK^T produces scores that Softmax can consume directly, and PV consumes the resulting probabilities, avoiding intermediate repacking. For nonlinear ops, we use minimax polynomial approximation with input-range control and joint error allocation guided by model quality, reducing polynomial degree and multiplicative depth. To our knowledge, Odin is the first open-source end-to-end GPU CKKS implementation of Llama-3. With Llama-3-8B weights and a 128-token input, Odin evaluates all 32 Transformer layers on a single NVIDIA H100 80 GB GPU. Server-side end-to-end FHE evaluation takes 366.4 s and 58.9 GiB peak device memory. Under the same model, input, CKKS parameters, and hardware, THOR takes 1651.9 s, a 4.51x speedup.
item.dc:creator: Yuhang Fan, Yusi Chen, Kanyu Ye, Zhuoran Ji

item.title: SecJev: Bringing Security Expertise to System One Decision Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.03073v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Security workflows need models that turn complex observations and explicit policies into decisions. System One models introduced by Jev return typed predictions and probabilities; security specialization supplies the domain expertise behind those predictions. We introduce SecJev, to our knowledge the first family of Jev-style decision models specialized for security, spanning 0.8B to 9B parameters. Built on Kev's single-pass candidate scorer, SecJev learns Boolean, choice, and ordered decisions from text, telemetry, and observation histories. We develop SecJev-Corpus to unify source-label prediction and explicit-policy evaluation across 14 tasks and eight sources. It covers tool outputs, traffic, federated updates, consensus, authentication, and vehicle messages. Scene-weighted training adapts the models across these domains while preserving a shared typed decision interface. Security specialization improves every model in the family; SecJev-0.8B outperforms general Kev-9B by 20.51 percentage points in task-macro accuracy. At 0.8B and 4B, SecJev achieves accuracy and latency close to answer-only generative fine-tuning with lower peak allocated GPU memory. SecJev-4B improves on Kev-4B and security-trained generation in prompt-injection and traffic transfer tests. We release adapters, decision heads, SecJev-Corpus, and training and inference code.
item.dc:creator: Zheng Chen, Fei Yu, Haohao Huang, Yang Li, Anlong Chen, Lei Chen

item.title: NOMOS: Compiling Written Policies into Statically Verified Tool-Call Gates for LLM Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.11030v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tool-using LLM agents violate the policies they are deployed to enforce, often silently. Prior defenses hand-write rules, query an LLM verifier per action, or compile policies through heavyweight formal machinery. Naive compilation fails: extracted rules block the tool satisfying their own precondition, or read arguments their tool lacks. NOMOS, a four-pass compiler, turns a natural-language policy into a deterministic tool-call gate; static verification with tool-schema-level checks alone (no prover, solver, or LLM) repairs or rejects 37% (airline) and 13% (retail) of candidates, without which most shipped rules are inoperable. Replaying compiled rules over undefended transcripts flags bindings that refuse legitimate work (a development binding refused 95.9% of task-passing calls); no evaluation binding is flagged. On $\tau^2$-bench the gate cuts violations of reference-encoded clauses among state-changing calls from 66.3% to 2.6% (airline) and 30.8% to 6.9% (retail), raising airline task success significantly for $2 \le k \le 4$; a 26B on-premise compilation is not significantly worse than hand-written or frontier-compiled rules. Unlike AgentDojo's shipped defenses, it reaches a zero attack success rate (ASR) on banking, where nine attack families collapse onto three structural rules. On the other three suites its ASR is at most 3.6%, from goals with no tool call to govern and one write admitted by a binding weaker than its clause; a second agent model, Llama-3.3-70B, reproduces the effect on both benchmarks. Decisions take microseconds without an LLM call, at a domain-dependent benign-utility cost; compilation runs on-premise on open-weight gemma-4-26B.
item.dc:creator: Min-Young Yu, Tony Kim, Jang Won Choi

item.title: Characterizing Statistical Separability in TP-CRIV for Probabilistic AI Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.11163v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Third-party challenge-response identity verification (TP-CRIV) enables an independent verifier to assess whether a claimant possesses a model identical to a remotely deployed model without directly accessing the reference model. However, for probabilistic AI models, repeated executions of the same query may produce different outputs and therefore different verification observations. This raises the question of how such stochastic evidence should be accumulated and how much evidence is required for reliable verification. In this work, we characterize statistical separability in TP-CRIV of probabilistic AI models. Specifically, we relate challenge-wise behavior of matching and non-matching provers to verification-level separability. The characterization explicitly describes how the numbers of independent challenges and repeated responses affect detection performance and enables the verification budget required for a target AUC to be estimated. We instantiate the proposed characterization for LLMs using open-ended challenges. The experiments demonstrate matching-non-matching separation, close agreement between theoretical and empirical AUCs, and consistent estimates of the minimum verification budgets. These results provide a statistical basis for relating probabilistic model behavior to verification-level separability and the evidence required for third-party verification.
item.dc:creator: Teruki Sano, Minoru Kuribayashi, Masao Sakai, Shuji Isobe, Eisuke Koizumi, Zhang Zhang, Satoru Matsumoto

item.title: Natural Code Transformation Confuses Agents in Vulnerability Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.14350v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Having demonstrated a strong potential for automating vulnerability discovery, AI agents can also be used to attack software systems at scale. Today's software systems need mechanisms to level the playing field by slowing down potential attacks, giving them time to patch vulnerabilities and strengthen software. Along this line, our study of agent trajectories in vulnerability analysis shows a surprising finding: agents produce dramatically different results across real-world code commits that carry the same functionality and the same vulnerability. This phenomenon appears consistently in multiple code domains and vulnerability categories. It motivates us to study natural and functionality-preserving code transformations derived from real-world software development, and their potential as a defense against attacker agents. We build a corpus of natural transformations by mining recurring development patterns from real-world code commits, and apply them to evaluate impact on agentic vulnerability analysis. Our results show that even a single form of transformation can effectively "confuse" frontier agents, e.g., Codex with GPT-6 Sol, reducing successes in vulnerability discovery. We also study different agent failures, whether transformations can be composed to provide stronger protection, and adaptive attackers who seek to reverse them. Overall, our study of natural code transformation significantly expands the research space of using code transformations to defend against malicious agents.
item.dc:creator: Jie Zhu, Ronik Bhaskar, Heather Zheng, Ben Y. Zhao, Kexin Pei

item.title: SecReason: Vulnerability Detection and In-Stream Self-Repair for LLM Code Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14453v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) may introduce security vulnerabilities into generated code, which can persist into production when verification focuses on functional correctness. Existing defenses act before, during, or after generation, but none inspects the code during generation. Security prompts and retrieved security knowledge act before any code exists, constrained decoding limits token choices but cannot guide repair, and post-hoc repair must regenerate the full response. Reasoning LLMs draft code early in their streamed chain of thought, and in this pre-delivery window the code exists only inside the reasoning stream. We present SecReason, an in-stream defense that monitors this window. Dual-track incremental scanning applies security rules, checking each statement as it is emitted and tracing dataflows across the accumulated code. When a security rule fires, SecReason interrupts generation, inserts an in-stream warning, and resumes decoding, so the model repairs the draft within the same reasoning trace without regenerating the full response. On tasks where unassisted generation introduces vulnerabilities, \system raises the share of runs delivering secure and functionally correct code from below 15\% to 72.8\%--98.1\% on \tool{CWEval} and \tool{SecCodeBench}. \system consumes fewer tokens than post-hoc repair, and when security rules misfire on secure code, it limits the functional regressions from false warnings.
item.dc:creator: Ruidong Han, Zhensu Sun, Chengyan Ma, Yuqing Niu, Zhou Yang, Siqi Ma, David Lo

item.title: SkillMarker: A KGW-Based Watermarking Method for Agent Skill Ownership Verification
item.description: arXiv:2610.15725v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agent skills encode operational procedures and domain expertise as reusable knowledge assets, yet their distribution in plaintext exposes them to unauthorized copying and leakage. However, practical mechanisms for skill ownership verification and leakage tracing remain underdeveloped. Watermark embedding before distribution offers a potential solution, but structured, compact skill instructions impose stringent requirements for factual and procedural accuracy. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillMarker, a KGW-based watermarking method that jointly targets functionality preservation and strong watermark embedding. SkillMarker unifies quality-constrained rewriting with signal-oriented candidate search. The former separates essential knowledge from flexible expression to preserve instruction fidelity; the latter explores alternative expressions to obtain a stronger watermark signal under preservation constraints. We release an open-source toolkit that integrates watermark embedding, quality auditing, and detection to support the protection of agent skills. SkillMarker targets ownership verification and leakage tracing in distributed skill ecosystems, where content may be copied in whole or in part, or incorporated into other skills. Across four datasets, SkillMarker negligibly affects downstream task performance on average. In our copy-paste tests, window-based detection consistently identifies copied passages containing as few as 1,536 consecutive tokens. Even after merging with one or three background skills, SkillMarker retains watermark detection rates of 72.2--77.8\%.
item.dc:creator: Alan Tang, Lifeng Wang, Gang Wu, Tao Zhang, Yantao Jia, Xiaofeng Zhu

item.title: Doctor Trigger: A Framework for Release-Bound Face Verification
item.description: arXiv:2610.16336v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Face swapping and generative editing enable realistic facial manipulation, while online redistribution complicates publisher oversight of circulating face images. Existing approaches establish provenance, detect manipulation, recover embedded watermarks, verify image integrity, or disrupt unauthorized face manipulation. These capabilities do not necessarily establish consistency with a specific publisher-enrolled release, limiting the evidence available for verification and human review. To address this gap, we introduce Doctor Trigger, a framework for verifying circulating faces against private publisher-held release records. Before publication, the publisher embeds a weak keyed Fourier-phase signal in each face while preserving visual fidelity and stores its spectral reference. Afterward, verification compares the circulating face with that reference and uses key projection to measure retention of the release-specific signal. Therefore, relation and key evidence jointly help publishers identify suspicious copies for review, potentially reducing the circulation of manipulated images. Experimental results across FF++, DFDC, and Celeb-DF show that spectral agreement separates tested face swaps and generative manipulations from enrolled releases, while the keyed signal distinguishes published versions from their unreleased originals under the evaluated key-preserving benign transformations. Doctor Trigger complements provenance metadata with release-specific face verification and record-linked evidence for further assessment.
item.dc:creator: Chia-Ming Lee, Chia-Yu Lin, Hung-Kai Huang, Yi-Ting Ku, Yu-Chen Liang, Chih-Chung Hsu

item.title: Risk-aware Road-network Trajectory Synthesis under Local Differential Privacy
item.description: arXiv:2610.16384v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Road-network trajectory synthesis under local differential privacy (LDP) enables mobility data analysis without uploading raw trajectories to an untrusted server. Existing locally private trajectory synthesis methods mainly model whole trajectories, point sequences, or grid-level mobility patterns. However, they cannot handle non-uniform privacy risks caused by local road-network and trajectory contexts, such as endpoints, long-stay-associated regions, and low-out-degree branches. They also do not directly protect conditional next-hop choices on road networks, where a user's selected successor may reveal sensitive local movement intentions. To address these challenges, we propose TrajRACE, a locally private synthesis framework for road-network trajectories. TrajRACE uses start, segment-count, and transition reports to represent trajectories. For each transition, it keeps the current road segment as a public aggregation context and perturbs the true successor among legal successors on the client side. It then assigns risk-aware protection strengths to transitions according to local road-network and trajectory contexts. Finally, the server recovers population-level start, segment-count, and conditional transition statistics from heterogeneous privatized reports, and generates synthetic trajectories that follow the public road-network topology. Experiments on three road-network trajectory datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of TrajRACE in improving synthetic-data utility across distributional, query-based, and pattern-level metrics, while providing stronger protection for high-risk local transitions.
item.dc:creator: Hongzhen Xiang, Chenxu Wang, Yumeng Song, Tao Qin, Yushuai Li, Pinghui Wang, Wei Wang, Tianyi Li

item.title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.17727v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL$.$md in a single forward pass. On MaliciousSkillBench, SkillScreen flags 20-25% of benign skills at 99% recall on unseen attack families, substantially fewer than the word-level classifier and prompted LLM judges tested. Under the same training protocol, it also generalizes better than a fully fine-tuned encoder to unseen sources. Yet unfamiliar benign sources sharply increase false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not ensure reliable screening of new skill collections. Our results demonstrate the value of task-trained decision models for high-recall skill screening. Project page: https://jerroldh.github.io/SkillScreen-webpage/
item.dc:creator: Jerrold Huang, Junwei Quan, Saiyue Lyu, Zihan Guo, Yingqiang Ge

item.title: Privacy-Preserving GNN Inference on Financial Transaction Graphs via Homomorphic Encryption
item.description: arXiv:2610.18054v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Anti-money laundering (AML) in financial networks requires modeling transaction patterns that span multiple institutions. In practice, however, banks cannot share account and transaction features due to strict privacy regulations. We propose a privacy-preserving graph neural network (GNN) inference framework tailored to this multi-bank setting. A central server holds the graph connectivity and pretrained model weights in plaintext, while each bank keeps its transaction features encrypted. Inference is then carried out entirely on encrypted features under the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme, so that no plaintext transaction features or predictions are exposed to the server. The key to making this practical is an edge-centric GNN architecture, wherein message passing is expressed through operations on node--edge incidence matrices. This formulation not only preserves the edge-attributed multigraph structure of transaction networks but also reduces every aggregation step to plaintext--ciphertext matrix products. Since CKKS can evaluate only polynomial circuits, we also approximate each nonlinearity with a composite polynomial of the sign function, which we calibrate per activation site. On the IBM AML benchmark, our model achieves performance competitive with plaintext baselines, and with a consumer-grade GPU, classifies each queried transaction end-to-end in as little as 5.31 seconds, while per-transaction latency can be amortized to 1.65 seconds when optimized for throughput.
item.dc:creator: H. \c{C}a\u{g}r{\i} Bilgi, Kemal Mutluergil, Ceren Y{\i}ld{\i}r{\i}m, Kubilay Atasu, Erkay Savas

item.title: X.js: A Live Benchmark for Node.js Taint-Style Vulnerabilities
item.description: arXiv:2610.18585v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: JavaScript vulnerabilities in npm packages pose a significant risk to the Node$.$js ecosystem, and a growing body of work aims to detect, exploit, and mitigate them. Studying and evaluating this work requires up-to-date collections of real vulnerabilities, yet the most commonly used datasets stop recording vulnerabilities in 2022. We present X$.$js, a live benchmark of real-world Node$.$js taint-style vulnerabilities covering code and command injection, prototype pollution, and path traversal. Built from 1,738 advisories collected through mid-2026, primarily from the GitHub Advisory Database, X$.$js pairs each vulnerability with precise source and sink locations, a validated executable exploit and its execution trace, and, when available, a patched version of the package. X$.$js supports long-term reproducibility and growth: dependencies are mirrored in a self-hosted registry to guard against package removal from the ecosystem, and dedicated infrastructure generates and validates exploits for newly reported vulnerabilities. The current release contains 1,159 validated exploits for 965 packages. Using X$.$js, we characterize how the frequency, structure, and complexity of Node$.$js taint-style vulnerabilities have evolved over time. We find that these vulnerabilities are increasingly reported in large packages: the median vulnerable package grew from roughly 250 LoC in 2021--2022 to 6,100 LoC in 2026.
item.dc:creator: Jos\'e Afonso, Jo\~ao Madeira Pereira, Ronghao Ni, Limin Jia, Jos\'e Fragoso Santos, Pedro Ad\~ao

item.title: Noise-Aware Differentially Private Variational Inference
item.description: arXiv:2410.19371v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Differential privacy (DP) provides robust privacy guarantees for statistical inference, but this can lead to unreliable results and biases in downstream applications. While several noise-aware approaches have been proposed which integrate DP perturbation into the inference, they are limited to specific types of simple probabilistic models. In this work, we propose a novel method for noise-aware approximate Bayesian inference based on stochastic gradient variational inference which can also be applied to high-dimensional and non-conjugate models. We also propose a more accurate evaluation method for noise-aware posteriors. Empirically, our inference method has similar performance to existing methods in the domain where they are applicable. Outside this domain, we obtain accurate coverages on high-dimensional Bayesian linear regression and well-calibrated predictive probabilities on Bayesian logistic regression with the UCI Adult dataset.

item.title: Majority Bit-Aware Watermarking For Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2508.03829v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The growing deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) has raised concerns about their misuse in generating harmful or deceptive content. To address this issue, watermarking methods have been proposed to embed identifiable multi-bit messages into generated text for misuse tracing. However, existing methods often suffer from a fundamental trade-off between text quality and decoding accuracy. In particular, they have to restrict the size of the preferred token set (i.e., green list) during encoding to maintain a detectable watermark signal for decoding, which inevitably degrades generation quality. To improve this trade-off, we propose a novel message encoding paradigm called \textit{majority bit-aware encoding}, which relaxes the watermark signal strength from the green list size. This strategy allows for a strong watermark signal to be preserved in generated texts even when using a large green list. We introduce two instantiations of this paradigm: MajorMark and MajorMark$^{+}$, where the latter is specifically optimized for long messages. Extensive experiments on state-of-the-art LLMs demonstrate that our methods achieve higher decoding accuracy and superior text quality compared to prior baselines. The code is at https://github.com/JiiahaoXU/MajorMark.

item.title: How Feasible are Passive Network Attacks on 5G Networks and Beyond? A Survey
item.description: arXiv:2512.20622v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Privacy concerns around 5G, the latest generation of mobile networks, are growing, with fears that its deployment may increase exposure to privacy risks. This perception is largely driven by the use of denser deployments of small antenna systems, which enable highly accurate data collection at higher speeds and closer proximity to mobile users. At the same time, 5G's unique radio communication features can make the reproduction of known network attacks more challenging. In particular, passive network attacks, which do not involve direct interaction with the target network and are therefore nearly impossible to detect, remain a pressing concern. Such attacks can reveal sensitive information about users, their devices, and active applications, which may then be exploited through known vulnerabilities or spear-phishing schemes. This survey examines the feasibility of passive network attacks in 5G and beyond (B5G/6G) networks, with emphasis on two major categories: information extraction (system identification, website and application fingerprinting) and geolocation (user identification and position tracking). These attacks are well documented and reproducible in existing wireless and mobile systems, including short-range networks (IEEE 802.11) and, to a lesser extent, LTE. Current evidence suggests that while such attacks remain theoretically possible in 5G, their practical execution is significantly constrained by directional beamforming, high-frequency propagation characteristics, and encryption mechanisms. For B5G and early 6G networks, the lack of public tools and high hardware cost currently renders these attacks infeasible in practice, which highlights a critical gap in our understanding of future network threat models.

item.title: A quantum algorithm for one-shot signatures
item.description: arXiv:2606.23612v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We provide a pre-obfuscation circuit-level implementation of an efficient one shot signature scheme, which has known applications to delegated signatures, secure token transfer, and publicly verifiable randomness. The algorithm consists of two stages: a key generation stage where a classical public key/quantum secret key pair is produced, and a signing stage where the quantum secret key is processed with a message string to produce a classical signature. There is no algorithmic error in the construction and the signed message can be efficiently checked by a classical verifier. Our scheme works by preparing a superposition over elements of a random affine coset determined by the output of a puncturable pseudorandom function, together with a circuit that tests coset membership. The logical qubit number scales like $\Theta( \kappa\log(r) + n + l)$ and the gate complexity scales like $\Theta(n^3 + nl)$, where $r$ is the public key size, $n+l$ is the signature size, $l$ is the message size, and $\kappa = \Omega(n)$ is the cryptographic security parameter. We provide explicit qubit and gate counts before obfuscation. A secure instantiation additionally requires modified key generation and a security proof for the resulting obfuscated construction.

item.title: Same Request, Different Boundary: Evaluating Cybersecurity Assistance across Conversational Contexts
item.description: arXiv:2609.00578v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cybersecurity assistance is dual use, requiring decisions about when to answer, limit, or refuse a request. Prior work studies refusal evaluation and conversational jailbreaking, but how conversational histories shift assistance boundaries in both directions for identical cybersecurity requests remains underexplored. We introduce 3R-Bench, a benchmark of 150 real-world cybersecurity requests evaluated across eight LLMs under direct prompting and two predefined conversational settings. We separately code refusal, bounded assistance, compliance, and provider blocking to characterize delivered assistance. On 400 matched ambiguous request-model pairs, compliance is 75.3% directly, 57.8% after refused precedent, and 81.0% after accepted precedent. A smaller repeated-generation panel reproduces the refusal-acceptance gap. On a balanced 75-request panel reusing the direct baseline, compliance decreases from 74.2% directly to 57.2% after neutral task-decomposition dialogue and 60.3% after failure-ended dialogue. These findings show that cybersecurity assistance varies with conversational history and model deployment, motivating evaluation beyond direct-request refusal rates.

item.title: AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities
item.description: arXiv:2610.13928v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training, using a small chemical reaction prediction task as a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. We release our models to support the improvement of defenses.

item.title: Fast Forgiving Base64 Decoding with SIMD Instructions
item.description: arXiv:2610.17406v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: On the Internet, we use the Base64 format to represent binary data (e.g., images or cryptographic keys) as text. The ES2026 JavaScript standard, following the WHATWG forgiving-base64 rules, requires decoders to ignore ASCII whitespace while rejecting other non-alphabet characters. Prior SIMD Base64 decoders assume whitespace-free input. We present a block-oriented decoding algorithm that removes whitespace inside the SIMD loop: clean 64-character blocks are decoded directly, while blocks with ignorable characters are compacted into a small stack buffer. We provide implementations for x64 (SSSE3 through AVX-512 VBMI2), ARM NEON, and LoongArch. Our C++ decoder reaches up to 94 GB/s on recent AMD Zen 5 processors. In Node 25, integration of our decoder raises Uint8Array.fromBase64 throughput by up to 6x compared with Node 19. The implementation has been adopted by major browsers and JavaScript runtimes.
